screens.title: Handling Transaction ID Wraparound and Database Corruption
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on two critical operational risks for PostgreSQL: transaction ID wraparound and physical database corruption. You will learn what causes XID wraparound, why PostgreSQL freezes old transactions, and how autovacuum and VACUUM FREEZE work together to keep visibility rules correct. We will also cover the practical signals that warn you an XID problem is approaching, and the proactive tuning steps you can take to avoid emergencies. The second half addresses corruption: how to recognize page or index corruption from log messages, how to safely confirm damage with tools like data checksums and pg_checksums, and the recovery options ranging from logical dump salvage to full physical restore and point-in-time recovery. Each section emphasizes safe procedures, for example stopping the server before running low-level checks, and always working on copies of data files. By the end of the lesson you'll know how to monitor XID age, tune autovacuum aggressively when needed, perform an emergency VACUUM FREEZE, and follow the right diagnostics and backup-first recovery steps if corruption occurs.

Monitor and interpret

SHOW data_checksums;
pg_checksums -D /var/lib/postgresql/data --check

screens.title: What is Transaction ID (XID) Wraparound?
screens.narratorSegment: Transaction ID wraparound refers to a situation where PostgreSQL's 32-bit transaction counter cycles back toward zero after roughly four billion transactions. Each committed transaction receives a monotonically increasing XID. Over time, tuples created or updated by old transactions become dead rows until VACUUM removes them or marks them as frozen. Freezing marks tuples as belonging to transactions so old that their XID no longer participates in normal comparison logic. The problem arises when unfrozen XIDs remain near the counter wrap point. If the counter cycles, newly issued XIDs could be numerically less than those old, unfrozen XIDs, which breaks the numeric comparisons MVCC uses to decide visibility. That mismatch can cause transactions to see incorrect rows and could lead to silent data corruption or PostgreSQL taking protective measures, such as making the database read-only or refusing to start. A common misconception is thinking wraparound is only a performance issue; it is primarily an integrity hazard. For example, if a busy table receives many updates but autovacuum is starved, age(relfrozenxid) will grow and eventually trigger urgent warnings. Key takeaway: XID wraparound is an integrity risk that requires proactive monitoring and timely freezing of old tuples to protect visibility rules.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › What is XID Wraparound?
Core Concept

32-bit counter and frozen tuples

PostgreSQL assigns a 32-bit transaction ID to every commit. VACUUM marks very old transactions as frozen so they no longer need comparison logic. If freezing lags, wraparound can make new XIDs appear older than existing rows.

How visibility breaks
  • MVCC uses XID comparisons to decide which rows are visible to a transaction.
  • If new XIDs wrap and become numerically smaller, comparisons can be wrong.
  • This can cause incorrect read visibility and possible corruption of logical state.
Concrete example
A table with heavy updates that disables autovacuum can increase relfrozenxid rapidly. If values approach autovacuum_freeze_max_age, PostgreSQL will warn or block service to avoid wraparound.
Key Takeaway

Wraparound is an integrity risk, not just a performance issue. Freeze old XIDs before the counter nears its limit.

Misconception
Some teams assume vacuuming is optional for busy systems. In fact, vacuuming and freezing are vital to preserve correct visibility; neglecting them invites data integrity incidents.
Check this
Ask: When was the last time autovacuum completed on my largest tables? If unknown, monitor age(relfrozenxid).
Analogy
Think of XIDs like calendar dates without years. After 31 December, the counter goes to 1 January and you must rely on freezing (tagging) to remember which events happened long ago.

screens.title: How PostgreSQL Prevents Wraparound
screens.narratorSegment: PostgreSQL is built with protections against wraparound that rely on regular vacuuming and a specialized freeze process. Autovacuum runs in the background and performs regular VACUUM operations to remove dead tuples and eventually freeze very old transaction IDs. As a table's relfrozenxid approaches autovacuum_freeze_max_age, autovacuum enters an aggressive mode: it schedules more frequent freeze passes, and it will escalate warnings in the logs. The system parameter autovacuum_freeze_max_age defines the age threshold at which autovacuum is forced to act; its default is 200 million transactions. The process chain looks like this: normal vacuuming removes dead tuples, then freezing marks tuples as permanently old; monitoring keeps an eye on age(datfrozenxid) and age(relfrozenxid); and if warnings appear, operations teams must tune autovacuum or run manual vacuum freeze. A common operational mistake is assuming autovacuum always has enough resources; in high-transaction systems you must increase workers or reduce throttling so freeze work can complete before the counter nears wrap. The core idea: autovacuum prevents wraparound by freeing and freezing old XIDs, but it needs the right resources and tuning. How PostgreSQL Prevents Wraparound means autovacuum removes dead tuples and freezes old xids; tuning ensures it completes freeze work before wraparound.. In practical terms, autovacuum's role and the aggressive freeze phase. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › How PostgreSQL Prevents Wraparound
Process Flow

Autovacuum → Freeze → Warnings

Normal VACUUM
Removes dead tuples and reclaims space for reuse.
Freezing
Marks very old XIDs as frozen so they no longer need comparison checks.
Aggressive autovacuum
When age approaches autovacuum_freeze_max_age, autovacuum runs more often and warns in logs.
Operational signals
  • Log warnings that a database or table must be vacuumed within N transactions.
  • High values returned by age(datfrozenxid) or age(relfrozenxid).
  • Autovacuum processes not visible in pg_stat_activity or taking too long to finish.
Misconception
Believing that autovacuum will always catch up without tuning. In heavy-change environments, autovacuum must be given enough workers and less throttle to do its freeze work.
Key Takeaway

Autovacuum prevents wraparound, but it must be properly resourced and tuned for busy databases.

screens.title: Monitoring XID Age and Autovacuum Activity
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring XID age is the practical first step to preventing wraparound. There are two key system columns: datfrozenxid for databases and relfrozenxid for relations. Use age() around those values to get human-friendly ages in transaction counts. Typical monitoring queries return the top databases and tables by age so you can target attention. For example, select datname and age(datfrozenxid) from pg_database ordered by age descending; similarly query pg_class for relfrozenxid to see the most aged tables. Interpretation: if age values consistently exceed about 150 million, autovacuum may be struggling. Warnings in logs like must be vacuumed within N transactions are explicit signals you should not ignore. Also check pg_stat_activity to confirm autovacuum worker presence and completion frequency. A common pitfall is inspecting only average activity; you must look at the oldest relations which might be starved for vacuuming. Use these queries regularly and set alerts when ages cross a chosen threshold to allow time for corrective tuning or maintenance VACUUM FREEZE. Monitoring XID Age and Autovacuum Activity means regularly run age(datfrozenxid) and age(relfrozenxid) queries and alert before values approach autovacuum_freeze_max_age.. In practical terms, queries and interpretation to spot at-risk databases and tables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Monitoring XID Age
Monitoring

Key queries to run regularly

-- Monitor XID age for all databases
SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) AS xid_age,
       (SELECT setting FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'autovacuum_freeze_max_age')::int - age(datfrozenxid) AS remaining_xids_to_freeze_max_age
FROM pg_database
ORDER BY xid_age DESC;

-- Monitor XID age for tables
SELECT relname, age(relfrozenxid) AS xid_age,
       (SELECT setting FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'autovacuum_freeze_max_age')::int - age(relfrozenxid) AS remaining_xids_to_freeze_max_age
FROM pg_class
WHERE relkind = 'r'
ORDER BY xid_age DESC
LIMIT 20;
Interpretation tips
  • If remaining_xids_to_freeze_max_age becomes small, schedule corrective action.
  • Focus on tables with the highest relfrozenxid ages; global averages hide hot tables.
  • Use pg_stat_activity to confirm autovacuum processes are running and finishing.
Concrete example
If age(relfrozenxid) returns 190,000,000 and autovacuum_freeze_max_age is 200,000,000, there's only a small window left. Tune autovacuum or run manual vacuum freeze quickly.
Common Mistake

Ignoring long-running autovacuum or assuming one worker will keep up. Increase workers if many tables need attention.

screens.title: Autovacuum Tuning Options
screens.narratorSegment: When autovacuum struggles to keep XIDs frozen, selective tuning can restore safety. There are global parameters and table-level overrides. Key global settings include autovacuum_max_workers to increase parallelism, autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay to reduce throttling, and autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor and autovacuum_vacuum_threshold to change how often vacuum triggers. For very busy tables, table-level settings allow fine control without overloading the cluster; for example, setting autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to a very small value on a hot table causes more frequent vacuum runs for that table alone. A useful heuristic: if many tables are aged, increase max workers; if autovacuum is too slow on individual hot tables, reduce scale factor and threshold or run manual VACUUM FREEZE in a planned window. A common pitfall is setting cost_delay to zero across the board without considering IO impact; balance is important. Always monitor the result: check age(relfrozenxid) drops and ensure autovacuum workers are not just queued. The practical plan is incremental: raise workers, reduce cost delay moderately, then lower scale factors for specific problem tables. Autovacuum Tuning Options means combine global increases in resources with targeted per-table aggressiveness and monitor the results to prevent wraparound.. In practical terms, which parameters to change and why — global vs table-level settings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Autovacuum Tuning Options
Comparison

Global settings vs table-level overrides

Global tuning
  • autovacuum_max_workers: more workers for concurrency.
  • autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay: reduce to make autovacuum less throttled.
  • Scale factors/thresholds apply cluster-wide defaults.
Table-level tuning
  • ALTER TABLE ... SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.001) for hot tables.
  • Controls frequency for specific problem relations without global cost.
  • Use when a few heavy tables drive the risk.
Example command
ALTER TABLE my_busy_table SET (
  autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.001
);
Pro Tip
Apply global increases first, then target problematic tables. Monitor system IO to avoid swapping autovacuum into latency problems.
Key Takeaway

Tune both globally and per-table; prefer incremental changes and monitor age() metrics to verify improvement.

screens.title: When and How to Run VACUUM FREEZE
screens.narratorSegment: VACUUM FREEZE is the emergency measure to prevent imminent wraparound by forcing freezing of old transaction IDs up to the current point. Because it marks tuples as permanently frozen, it stops XID ageing for those rows. However, VACUUM FREEZE can be a blocking operation on the table(s) it processes, so run it during a maintenance window when possible. Use VACUUM FREEZE VERBOSE my_table to monitor progress and confirm the relfrozenxid age resets to a low value afterwards. If many tables are affected, running VACUUM FREEZE for the entire database is possible from a superuser connection, but expect significant input and output and locking. A common operational mistake is running VACUUM FREEZE on production tables during peak hours without sufficient coordination; the blocking nature can cause application outages. Before initiating, ensure you have backups and communicate the maintenance window. After a successful VACUUM FREEZE, re-enable or retune autovacuum so normal freeze work continues automatically and the emergency operation isn't repeatedly needed. When and How to Run VACUUM FREEZE means vacuum freeze forces freezing to prevent wraparound but can block; schedule it carefully and verify relfrozenxid reset.. In practical terms, emergency freezing, blocking behavior, and safe scheduling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Emergency Procedure

Planning and execution

Before running VACUUM FREEZE, pick a maintenance window and ensure backups exist. VACUUM FREEZE marks tuples as frozen and is blocking on the tables it touches.

Command example
VACUUM FREEZE VERBOSE my_critical_table;
-- Or from a superuser for the whole database (blocking):
-- VACUUM FREEZE VERBOSE;
  • Run during maintenance to avoid application impact.
  • Verify relfrozenxid is reset after completion.
  • Retune autovacuum so this is not repeatedly required.
Checklist
  1. Confirm backups and notify stakeholders.
  2. Choose maintenance window and target tables.
  3. Run VACUUM FREEZE VERBOSE and monitor logs.
Warning

VACUUM FREEZE can block queries; do not run it on production hot paths without coordination.

screens.title: Database Corruption: What It Means and Common Causes
screens.narratorSegment: Database corruption means the physical data files are inconsistent or damaged so PostgreSQL cannot read pages or indexes correctly. Common error messages include invalid page header, could not read block, or index contains unexpected data. Causes are often environmental: disk hardware failures, faulty R A M, filesystem bugs, sudden power loss, or misconfigured OS settings that prevent proper fsync behavior. Application-level mistakes like accidental deletion of data files also cause corruption. PostgreSQL features such as full_page_writes and fsync are designed to protect against partial page writes during crashes; disabling them increases risk. A misconception is to assume corruption always originates inside PostgreSQL; more often the root cause is hardware, OS, or storage misconfiguration. Understanding likely causes helps prioritize actions: if you had a power outage and full_page_writes was off, partial page writes are a likely culprit. The immediate reaction to suspected corruption should be conservative: stop the database to avoid further damage and preserve state for diagnostics. Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Database Corruption
Definition

Symptoms and common causes

Example log messages
"invalid page header in block 12345 of relation base/..." or "could not read block"
Likely root causes
  • Hardware failures: disk or memory errors.
  • OS or filesystem problems preventing fsync.
  • Power loss with full_page_writes disabled or failing fsync.
  • Rare bugs or manual file tampering.
Immediate action
If you suspect corruption, stop the database immediately to avoid further writes and preserve state for diagnostics.
Key Takeaway

Corruption is typically environmental; protective settings like full_page_writes and checksums reduce risk and improve detection.

screens.title: Steps to Diagnose Suspected Corruption Safely
screens.narratorSegment: Diagnosing corruption is a surgical process: stop the server, verify, and then decide on salvage or restore. The first step is to stop the database to prevent additional writes. If data checksums were enabled at initdb time, use pg_checksums to verify data pages; this is reliable for block-level corruption detection but requires the server to be stopped. Next, try a logical dump with pg_dumpall or pg_dump. A logical dump may still read some tables even if others are corrupt, which lets you salvage unaffected data. Use pg_filedump or community tools to inspect individual data files if needed. Throughout, work on copies of the data directory; never attempt low-level fixes on original files. If corruption is localized and noncritical, consider dumping the readable tables, reinitializing a clean cluster, and importing the good data. If corruption is widespread, restore from physical backups and WAL archives. Key misconception: a successful pg_dump does not guarantee all indexes or pages are intact; it only shows that particular reads succeeded. Always combine checksum results, dump attempts, and log analysis to form a recovery plan. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Diagnosing Corruption
Diagnosis

Safe, ordered steps

Step 1 — Stop the server
Prevent further writes to preserve the current on-disk state for inspection.
Step 2 — Verify checksums
If data checksums were enabled, run pg_checksums to detect corrupted pages at block level.
Step 3 — Attempt logical dumps
Use pg_dump or pg_dumpall to salvage readable tables. Logical dumps may succeed for some objects even when others fail.
Commands to run
-- Check checksums (requires DB stopped)
pg_checksums -D /var/lib/postgresql/data --check

-- Logical dump to salvage readable data
pg_dump -Fc -f mydatabase_backup.dump mydatabase
pg_dumpall -f all_databases.sql
Common Pitfall

Do not try to edit data files directly; always work on copies and prefer logical extraction where possible.

screens.title: Recovery Options: Salvage vs Full Restore
screens.narratorSegment: When corruption is confirmed, teams must choose between salvaging readable data and performing a full physical restore. Salvage attempts begin with pg_dump or pg_dumpall to extract any intact tables and objects; this approach is useful when corruption is localized and you lack a recent physical backup. If the corruption is widespread or involves critical system catalogs, the reliable option is to restore from a known-good base backup and replay WAL archives to a point-in-time just before the incident. Point-in-Time Recovery requires a valid physical base backup and continuous WAL archiving. If neither is available, the salvage process can still recover some data but may require reinitializing the cluster and accepting partial loss. Always work on copies and never overwrite the original broken cluster before you have exhausted recovery options. After recovery, perform a root cause analysis and address the underlying cause—replace faulty hardware, correct filesystem settings, and ensure full_page_writes and checksums are enabled where possible. The practical guidance: prefer full physical restore and PITR when available; use logical dumps to salvage when needed. Recovery Options: Salvage vs Full Restore means prefer restoring from physical backups and wal archives for full recovery; use logical dumps to salvage partial data if backups are missing.. Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Recovery Options
Architecture

Salvage vs Restore

Salvage with logical dump
Try pg_dump or pg_dumpall to extract unaffected tables. Useful when corruption is limited and no fresh physical backup exists.
Full physical restore and PITR
Restore a base backup and replay WAL archives up to a point just before corruption. Requires base backups and WAL archive policy.
When to choose which
  • Use PITR for complete recovery and consistency when backups exist.
  • Use logical dumps to salvage what you can when backups are absent or partial.
  • Reinitialize cluster and import good data if corruption reached system catalogs.
Commands
-- Logical backup
pg_dump -Fc -f mydatabase_backup.dump mydatabase
-- Full physical backup (example tool)
pg_basebackup -D /var/lib/postgresql/base -Ft -z
Key Takeaway

PITR with a good base backup and WAL archives is the most robust recovery; logical dumps are a salvage path when backups are incomplete.

screens.title: Operational Checklist to Reduce Risk
screens.narratorSegment: Long-term safety comes from a combination of configuration, redundancy, and tested procedures. Enable data checksums at initdb so you can detect block-level corruption with pg_checksums. Ensure full_page_writes is on to protect against partial page writes during crashes. Maintain a robust backup strategy: regular physical base backups plus continuous WAL archiving to allow point-in-time recovery. Regularly test your backups by restoring them to a staging environment so you know they are usable. Avoid disabling safety features like fsync or full_page_writes for performance gains unless you accept increased corruption risk. Finally, include these checks and procedures in your operational runbook so teams can execute them during incidents. Concrete configuration and operational items

screens.title: Hands-on: Simulate XID Ageing and Recover
screens.narratorSegment: This lab lets you observe how relfrozenxid behaves when autovacuum is temporarily disabled for a test table. Work only on a test instance. Create a table with a serial primary key and insert initial rows. Disable autovacuum for the table and run many update transactions to generate new XIDs; each update consumes a transaction ID and will increase the relfrozenxid age for that relation. Periodically run SELECT relname, age(relfrozenxid) FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'xid_test'; to observe the age rising. Once you see significant growth or log warnings, perform VACUUM FREEZE VERBOSE xid_test during a maintenance window. After completion, confirm the age has reset to a low value. Finally, re-enable autovacuum and drop the table. Remember the warning: do not do this on production. A common misunderstanding is to think a few thousand simulated transactions produce wraparound; they do not, but they show the mechanism and let you confirm autovacuum behavior and the effect of manual freeze. keyIdea.text: On a test instance, disable autovacuum for a table, generate many updates to raise relfrozenxid, then run VACUUM FREEZE and verify age resets.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Simulate XID Aging
Hands-on Activity

Safe simulation on a test DB

CREATE TABLE xid_test (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  data TEXT
);

ALTER TABLE xid_test SET (autovacuum_enabled = off);

-- Insert initial data
INSERT INTO xid_test (data) SELECT md5(random()::text) FROM generate_series(1, 10000);

-- Perform many updates inside a DO block to simulate transactions
DO $$
BEGIN
  FOR i IN 1..10000 LOOP
    UPDATE xid_test SET data = md5(random()::text) WHERE id = (random() * 9999 + 1)::int;
  END LOOP;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- Emergency corrective action
VACUUM FREEZE VERBOSE xid_test;

-- Cleanup
ALTER TABLE xid_test SET (autovacuum_enabled = on);
DROP TABLE xid_test;
Observation
After the updates, relfrozenxid age should rise. After VACUUM FREEZE, relfrozenxid age should return to a small value, showing the freeze effect.
Safety Note

Do not perform this simulation on production. The exercise demonstrates behavior and tools, not a production procedure.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Corruption and Recovery
screens.narratorSegment: These three key concepts summarize corruption detection and recovery. Database corruption describes physical damage or inconsistencies in data files, often signaled by invalid page headers or read errors. Data checksums are an initdb option that stores checksums on pages so you can detect corruption with pg_checksums; they must be enabled when the cluster is created. Point-in-Time Recovery is the process of restoring from a physical base backup and replaying WAL archives to a specific point before the incident; it is the most robust way to recover if corruption is detected. Keep in mind: checksums help you detect damage early, PITR lets you restore consistent state when you have proper backups and WAL archiving, and logical dumps can salvage readable objects when a full physical restore is not available. These mechanisms combined with good operational practices greatly reduce the risk of permanent data loss.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on two critical operational risks for PostgreSQL: transaction ID wraparound and physical database corruption. You will learn what causes XID wraparound, why PostgreSQL freezes old transactions, and how autovacuum and VACUUM FREEZE work together to keep visibility rules correct. We will also cover the practical signals that warn you an XID problem is approaching, and the proactive tuning steps you can take to avoid emergencies. The second half addresses corruption: how to recognize page or index corruption from log messages, how to safely confirm damage with tools like data checksums and pg_checksums, and the recovery options ranging from logical dump salvage to full physical restore and point-in-time recovery. Each section emphasizes safe procedures, for example stopping the server before running low-level checks, and always working on copies of data files. By the end of the lesson you'll know how to monitor XID age, tune autovacuum aggressively when needed, perform an emergency VACUUM FREEZE, and follow the right diagnostics and backup-first recovery steps if corruption occurs.

These learning objectives focus on operational competence. First, you will be able to explain how PostgreSQL's 32-bit transaction ID counter works, why transactions must be frozen, and why wraparound can corrupt visibility rules. Second, you will learn to identify early warning signs using logs and system views such as age(datfrozenxid) and age(relfrozenxid). Third, you'll gain practical skills to tune autovacuum, including both global parameters and table-level overrides, and when to run a manual VACUUM FREEZE during emergencies. Finally, you will understand how to detect physical corruption, use checksums and tools safely, and plan a recovery path that prioritizes restoring from known-good backups. Each objective is framed so you can both explain the root cause and perform safe practical actions during an incident. Learning Objectives means explain xid mechanics, monitor and tune autovacuum, and follow safe diagnosis and recovery steps for corruption.. In practical terms, what you'll be able to do after this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This second objectives slide drills into measurable skills and operational signals. You will practice running the two core monitoring queries for XID age and learn how to interpret their outputs to decide whether autovacuum is keeping up. You will also be able to tune autovacuum parameters like max workers, vacuum cost delay, scale factor and thresholds, including when to override settings for a single busy table. In emergency scenarios you'll learn when VACUUM FREEZE is required and how to schedule it to avoid blocking critical workloads. Finally, you'll know the right sequence for diagnosing suspected corruption: stop the server, run checksum verification if available, attempt logical dumps to salvage readable tables, and restore from physical backups for full recovery. These are hands-on skills you can apply in a maintenance window or incident response playbook.

Transaction ID wraparound refers to a situation where PostgreSQL's 32-bit transaction counter cycles back toward zero after roughly four billion transactions. Each committed transaction receives a monotonically increasing XID. Over time, tuples created or updated by old transactions become dead rows until VACUUM removes them or marks them as frozen. Freezing marks tuples as belonging to transactions so old that their XID no longer participates in normal comparison logic. The problem arises when unfrozen XIDs remain near the counter wrap point. If the counter cycles, newly issued XIDs could be numerically less than those old, unfrozen XIDs, which breaks the numeric comparisons MVCC uses to decide visibility. That mismatch can cause transactions to see incorrect rows and could lead to silent data corruption or PostgreSQL taking protective measures, such as making the database read-only or refusing to start. A common misconception is thinking wraparound is only a performance issue; it is primarily an integrity hazard. For example, if a busy table receives many updates but autovacuum is starved, age(relfrozenxid) will grow and eventually trigger urgent warnings. Key takeaway: XID wraparound is an integrity risk that requires proactive monitoring and timely freezing of old tuples to protect visibility rules.

PostgreSQL is built with protections against wraparound that rely on regular vacuuming and a specialized freeze process. Autovacuum runs in the background and performs regular VACUUM operations to remove dead tuples and eventually freeze very old transaction IDs. As a table's relfrozenxid approaches autovacuum_freeze_max_age, autovacuum enters an aggressive mode: it schedules more frequent freeze passes, and it will escalate warnings in the logs. The system parameter autovacuum_freeze_max_age defines the age threshold at which autovacuum is forced to act; its default is 200 million transactions. The process chain looks like this: normal vacuuming removes dead tuples, then freezing marks tuples as permanently old; monitoring keeps an eye on age(datfrozenxid) and age(relfrozenxid); and if warnings appear, operations teams must tune autovacuum or run manual vacuum freeze. Monitoring XID age is the practical first step to preventing wraparound. There are two key system columns: datfrozenxid for databases and relfrozenxid for relations. When autovacuum struggles to keep XIDs frozen, selective tuning can restore safety. There are global parameters and table-level overrides. Key global settings include autovacuum_max_workers to increase parallelism, autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay to reduce throttling, and autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor and autovacuum_vacuum_threshold to change how often vacuum triggers. For very busy tables, table-level settings allow fine control without overloading the cluster; for example, setting autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to a very small value on a hot table causes more frequent vacuum runs for that table alone. A useful heuristic: if many tables are aged, increase max workers; if autovacuum is too slow on individual hot tables, reduce scale factor and threshold or run manual VACUUM FREEZE in a planned window. A common pitfall is setting cost_delay to zero across the board without considering IO impact; balance is important. Always monitor the result: check age(relfrozenxid) drops and ensure autovacuum workers are not just queued. VACUUM FREEZE is the emergency measure to prevent imminent wraparound by forcing freezing of old transaction IDs up to the current point. Because it marks tuples as permanently frozen, it stops XID ageing for those rows. However, VACUUM FREEZE can be a blocking operation on the table(s) it processes, so run it during a maintenance window when possible. Use VACUUM FREEZE VERBOSE my_table to monitor progress and confirm the relfrozenxid age resets to a low value afterwards. If many tables are affected, running VACUUM FREEZE for the entire database is possible from a superuser connection, but expect significant input and output and locking. Before initiating, ensure you have backups and communicate the maintenance window. Database corruption means the physical data files are inconsistent or damaged so PostgreSQL cannot read pages or indexes correctly. Common error messages include invalid page header, could not read block, or index contains unexpected data. Causes are often environmental: disk hardware failures, faulty R A M, filesystem bugs, sudden power loss, or misconfigured OS settings that prevent proper fsync behavior. Application-level mistakes like accidental deletion of data files also cause corruption. PostgreSQL features such as full_page_writes and fsync are designed to protect against partial page writes during crashes; disabling them increases risk. A misconception is to assume corruption always originates inside PostgreSQL; more often the root cause is hardware, OS, or storage misconfiguration. Understanding likely causes helps prioritize actions: if you had a power outage and full_page_writes was off, partial page writes are a likely culprit. The immediate reaction to suspected corruption should be conservative: stop the database to avoid further damage and preserve state for diagnostics. Diagnosing corruption is a surgical process: stop the server, verify, and then decide on salvage or restore. The first step is to stop the database to prevent additional writes. If data checksums were enabled at initdb time, use pg_checksums to verify data pages; this is reliable for block-level corruption detection but requires the server to be stopped. Next, try a logical dump with pg_dumpall or pg_dump. A logical dump may still read some tables even if others are corrupt, which lets you salvage unaffected data. Use pg_filedump or community tools to inspect individual data files if needed. Throughout, work on copies of the data directory; never attempt low-level fixes on original files. If corruption is localized and noncritical, consider dumping the readable tables, reinitializing a clean cluster, and importing the good data. If corruption is widespread, restore from physical backups and WAL archives. Key misconception: a successful pg_dump does not guarantee all indexes or pages are intact; it only shows that particular reads succeeded. Always combine checksum results, dump attempts, and log analysis to form a recovery plan. When corruption is confirmed, teams must choose between salvaging readable data and performing a full physical restore. Salvage attempts begin with pg_dump or pg_dumpall to extract any intact tables and objects; this approach is useful when corruption is localized and you lack a recent physical backup. If the corruption is widespread or involves critical system catalogs, the reliable option is to restore from a known-good base backup and replay WAL archives to a point-in-time just before the incident. Point-in-Time Recovery requires a valid physical base backup and continuous WAL archiving. If neither is available, the salvage process can still recover some data but may require reinitializing the cluster and accepting partial loss. Always work on copies and never overwrite the original broken cluster before you have exhausted recovery options. After recovery, perform a root cause analysis and address the underlying cause—replace faulty hardware, correct filesystem settings, and ensure full_page_writes and checksums are enabled where possible. Long-term safety comes from a combination of configuration, redundancy, and tested procedures. Enable data checksums at initdb so you can detect block-level corruption with pg_checksums. Ensure full_page_writes is on to protect against partial page writes during crashes. Maintain a robust backup strategy: regular physical base backups plus continuous WAL archiving to allow point-in-time recovery. Regularly test your backups by restoring them to a staging environment so you know they are usable. Monitor autovacuum metrics and XID ages routinely and set alerts when values approach your chosen safety thresholds. Use redundant storage and replace suspect hardware promptly. Avoid disabling safety features like fsync or full_page_writes for performance gains unless you accept increased corruption risk. Finally, include these checks and procedures in your operational runbook so teams can execute them during incidents. These three concepts condense the XID and autovacuum ideas you must remember. Transaction ID wraparound is the integrity risk that arises when the 32-bit XID counter cycles and unfrozen old transactions remain on disk. autovacuum_freeze_max_age is the configured threshold that causes autovacuum to become aggressive and start freezing old XIDs; monitor values approaching this limit and act promptly. datfrozenxid and relfrozenxid are the system values that indicate the oldest unfrozen XID for a database or a relation; use age() around them to track how close you are to the freeze threshold. These items are connected: autovacuum uses the freeze age settings to protect against wraparound, and monitoring the frozen XID values gives the signal to tune or run an emergency VACUUM FREEZE. Keep these terms in mind as you apply the monitoring and tuning steps in operational practice.

These three key concepts summarize corruption detection and recovery. Database corruption describes physical damage or inconsistencies in data files, often signaled by invalid page headers or read errors. Data checksums are an initdb option that stores checksums on pages so you can detect corruption with pg_checksums; they must be enabled when the cluster is created. Point-in-Time Recovery is the process of restoring from a physical base backup and replaying WAL archives to a specific point before the incident; it is the most robust way to recover if corruption is detected. Keep in mind: checksums help you detect damage early, PITR lets you restore consistent state when you have proper backups and WAL archiving, and logical dumps can salvage readable objects when a full physical restore is not available. These mechanisms combined with good operational practices greatly reduce the risk of permanent data loss.
